Congregational Bible pledge from 2 Timothy 3:16, call and response, then opening prayer (0:45:56)

Reading of all eleven verses before the verse-by-verse (0:48:01)

But here's the thing is I could be wrong' (1:06:29-1:11:17)

Restatement of the main idea verbatim and closing prayer (1:12:33-1:14:01)
outline_begg: VOLUME2/08 'The Coming of the Lord, Part Two' (1 Thess 5:1-8). Long prologue on views of history: Lily Tomlin's bag lady Trudy and 'I worry that there is no cosmic scheme of things'; Kris Kristofferson's 'help me make it through the night' as popular Epicureanism; Carl Henry on God holding mankind accountable; the US Secretary for Education and the teaching of history; statistics - one in twenty-five NT verses on the return of Christ.
Thesis: 'You don't need an accurate chronology. You need a biblical theology. For a preoccupation with chronology, minus theology will give you nothing else than a mythology.'
Three points, announced up front: (1) the curiosity to be avoided, (2) the identity to be affirmed, (3) the strategy to be adopted.

1. Curiosity to be avoided (vv.1-3): Matthew 24:44 and Robert Murray McCheyne's Wednesday Bible study question 'do you think Jesus Christ will come today?'; Mark 13:32; Acts 1:6-8 'get off the hill, get into the streets'; three words - SECRET (the burglar who does not post you a card saying 'the Tuesday after next we will be burgling your house'; Begg's own house was burgled), SUDDEN (verse 3, and the Glasgow shoe-shop story of not knowing whether the Braxton Hicks were real), SEPARATION (Matthew 24:40-41).

Date-setters as cautionary tales: John Napier the inventor of logarithms projecting 1700 (23 editions between 1688 and 1700, 'since 1700 it has not been selling particularly well'); the Late Great Planet Earth; the 1784 prediction published in 1785.

2. Identity to be affirmed (vv.4-5): 'but you, brothers', generically used; Ephesians 5:8 and 1 Peter 2:9; the Shakespeare/Van Gogh illustration - 'if the genius of Van Gogh could come and live in me, I could paint that kind of picture'; a long attack on moralism and externalism, 'the identity is key to the activity'; 'if you shine, no need of sign'; the neon 'ADULT' sign on Interstate 71 at the base of which is total darkness.

3. Strategy to be adopted (v.6): 'so then'; gregoreo as the root of the name Gregory - 'let's all be Gregorys'; nepho, self-controlled; moral purity (1 John 3:3, 'you coming in my house... listening to my music, watching my videos') and zealous evangelism (John 9:4); 'Somebody gave me two books since last Sunday. I'm not reading them.'
VOLUME2/09 'The Coming of the Lord, Part Three' (1 Thess 5:6-11). Opens with the yellowed 1982 Times of London advertisement 'The Christ is now here' read out at length.

Since we belong to the day, three imperatives: STAY AWAKE (the ICU nurse; falling asleep at the wheel; the late flight to San Antonio because 'the pilot's asleep'; 1 Peter 5:8; Gethsemane), GUARD YOUR HEART (the breastplate of faith and love; the centurion who must not sleep when the city does; Ephesians 6 uses righteousness, here faith and love), KEEP YOUR HEAD (the helmet - 'Doesn't it scare you to see people screeching down the freeway on motorbikes without helmets?', extended and returned to at the close).

What God has done (vv.9-10): a full treatment of wrath as God's settled, non-capricious reaction to sin, grounded in Ephesians 2:3; 'it was the wrath of God that made Calvary necessary... it was the love of God that made Calvary a reality'; the fire brigade at the door in the middle of the night - 'we've come to rescue you' / 'but I don't need rescue'; imputation; 'My hope is built on nothing less'; Zinzendorf's 'Bold shall I stand in that great day'; Rock of Ages; the devil at 'the front door of your head' answered with 'while sin no longer reigns in my life, it remains'.

The implication (v.11): oikodomeo - building, mending nets, resetting fractured bones; 'Which of us emerges from the race of the Christian life without a few spikes in the shins?'; 'how are you fine, how are you fine, fine, fine'; 'commit yourself to being an encourager in Parkside Church'; encourage each other WITH THESE WORDS, i.e. with Scripture - Psalm 46 read down the phone to someone whose daughter has a tumour; the true pastor must be a good theologian.

Closing epigram: 'you'll never know who you are till you find out who he is. And some of you are spending all your time trying to find yourself and then you'll go look for him. I want to tell you, meet him. You'll find yourself.'
outline_comparison: Partly the same skeleton, for the obvious reason that both men are walking through 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11 in Paul's order: dates you cannot know, then 'but you, brothers, are sons of light', then the summons to alertness and the armour, then the wrath/salvation contrast, then 'encourage one another'. That sequence is Paul's, not Begg's. Below that shared verse order the two sermons share almost nothing. Begg announces a memorable three-point rhetorical scheme ('the curiosity to be avoided, the identity to be affirmed, the strategy to be adopted') and spends nearly a third of Part Two on a philosophy-of-history prologue with Lily Tomlin, Kris Kristofferson and Carl Henry; the FBC preacher has no prologue of that kind, uses a Haddon-Robinson-style single 'main idea' sentence which he states at [00:47:16] and repeats verbatim at [01:12:49], and organises the sermon around a modern 'how do you identify?' hook. Begg's three headings for verse 8 (stay awake, guard your heart, keep your head) have no counterpart at FBC, and Begg's two set-piece illustrations for that verse - the motorbike helmet and the centurion - are entirely absent from FBC, which instead uses a firefighter. Conversely FBC devotes six minutes to material Begg never touches: the chronos/kairos word study, the Galilean wedding, the three Greek senses of 'sleep', and an extended personal excursus on pre-trib/mid-trib/post-trib as a non-essential doctrine. They are even reading different translations - FBC works from the NASB ('as to the times and the epochs, brethren'), Begg from the NIV ('about times and dates... brothers') - which is why the only long shared word-strings in the whole comparison are Bible verses.

original_material.summary: Essentially the whole sermon is the preacher's own. A mechanical n-gram scan of the sermon window (4,421 words) against all twenty-two Begg transcripts returns not one shared seven-word string that is not Scripture: every hit is 1 Thess 4:16-17, 5:2, 5:5, 5:9 or 5:11, or 'died for us so that whether we', i.e. text both men are reading aloud. No Begg illustration, joke, commentator quote, epigram, transition or heading appears at FBC, and no FBC illustration appears in Begg. The preacher supplies his own hook (date-setting and Revelation), his own quoted authority (an unnamed researcher on ~300 failed predictions), his own humour (a self-consciously bad Armageddon pun), his own cultural framing (identity language borrowed from the contemporary gender debate and turned against it), his own liturgical habit (the congregational 2 Timothy 3:16 pledge, 'as is my normal practice'), two of his own family stories, a cross-reference back to his own earlier sermon series, his own word studies, a candid personal excursus in which he concedes he may be wrong about the timing of the rapture, and a local landing that ties the passage to the church's series title and to two named local outreaches.

rating_rationale: This sermon is genuinely independent of Begg and is the cleanest internal control in the corpus. The machine alignment is empty and my own seven-word n-gram scan of the sermon window against all twenty-two Begg transcripts produces only Scripture matches - 1 Thess 4:16-17, 5:2, 5:5, 5:9-11 - which is exactly what two preachers reading the same passage should produce and is not evidence of anything. The two men are not even using the same translation: FBC reads the NASB ('as to the times and the epochs, brethren'), Begg the NIV ('about times and dates... brothers'), so a preacher working from Begg's manuscript would have had to re-key every quotation. Every load-bearing illustration is different and, more tellingly, Begg's most memorable ones are missing precisely where a dependent sermon would have used them: at verse 8 Begg spends four minutes on the motorbike helmet and returns to it as his closing image, while FBC disposes of the helmet in a single clause and reaches for a firefighter instead; at verse 3 both preachers tell a first-child labour story, but FBC's is a go bag and a T-shirt reading 'coach' in an American hospital and Begg's is Braxton Hicks in a Glasgow shoe shop. The FBC preacher also does several things Begg never does anywhere in the series - a chronos/kairos word study, the Galilean wedding, a congregational 2 Timothy 3:16 pledge, and a candid admission that he may be wrong about the timing of the rapture - and the one quotation he does borrow, the unnamed researcher's tally of roughly 300 failed date predictions, has no counterpart in Begg, whose date-setting examples are Napier, Hal Lindsey and a 1784 prediction published in 1785. The only convergences are the ones the text itself forces: both make identity the theme of verses 4-5, both note that 'sons' is generic and includes daughters, and both cross-reference the armour to Ephesians 6 - observations available in any commentary and reached here in different words, different order and different company.

caveats: The alignment file for this sermon is empty (0.0% coverage) and the best machine scores were 1.65% and below, i.e. noise; 'region_classification' is therefore {} by design, not by omission.

All shared word-strings I could find between this sermon and any Begg transcript are Bible text that both preachers read aloud (1 Thess 4:16-17, 5:2, 5:5, 5:9-11). Under the brief's rule, Scripture read aloud by both is not evidence of borrowing, and here it is literally the only overlap.

The captions are YouTube auto-generated and mangle proper nouns and Greek: 'Kronos'/'chyros' for chronos/kairos, 'Thessalon Thessalonica', 'Kellon'/'Kelland' for the same elementary school, 'grieavves' for 'grieves', 'Ephesians 6:es 10-18', 'livinging hope' in the song lyrics. Quoted excerpts preserve the caption text verbatim; occasional capitalised runs (e.g. 'FOR YOU YOURSELVES KNOW FULL well') are a caption artefact, not emphasis.

There are no [music] tags in this file. I identified the songs by their lyric content and repeated refrains ('I'm no longer a slave to fear', 'Living Hope', 'Great Are You Lord', 'Hallelujah', 'Choose Joy'); every one of them falls outside the 0:42:55-1:14:01 sermon window.

Some overlap of ideas is unavoidable and generic: 'the day of the Lord comes like a thief', 'sons of light', 'not appointed to wrath', armour language, and the pairing of 1 Thess 5 with Matthew 24 and Ephesians 6 are standard evangelical stock and appear in every commentary on the passage. I have treated none of these as evidence.

Two speakers must be kept apart in any report drawn from this file: the sermon (0:42:55-1:14:01) is preached by the rotating teacher whose wife is Sheila, while the invitation at 1:18:52-1:26:04 - including the Kurt and Ace story and the sinner's prayer - is Pastor Pat, the lead pastor, whose wife is Cindy. That closing segment was not assessed as part of this sermon.

Because this file is being used as the study's internal control, the relevant claim is narrow: this preacher, on this passage, on this date, is not using Begg. It says nothing about the other FBC sermons in the playlist, several of which are preached by different men.
